bp: Start with a professional searcher facing a long ranked list of documents. A patent examiner is looking for earlier inventions that may decide whether a new patent should be granted. A medical reviewer is looking for studies that may decide what evidence enters a systematic review. In both cases, search is not finished when the system returns results. A person still has to inspect documents one by one and eventually decide that reading more is no longer worth it. That stopping decision is the real object of the paper. Stopping too early can miss a document that matters for law, medicine, or scientific evidence. Stopping too late spends expert time on documents whose chance of changing the final decision is small. The paper asks for a stopping rule that respects the purpose of the search. Instead of treating every task as a race toward the same recall target, it asks what each extra document is expected to buy.
wh: The hard part is that the searcher does not know what remains unseen. If all relevant documents were already labeled, stopping would be easy. The searcher could count what was found, count what was missed, and choose perfectly. Real screening is different: after reviewing the top part of the list, the searcher only sees the documents already examined and whatever evidence the ranking system provides about the rest. Existing Technology-Assisted Review stopping rules try to hit a pre-specified recall target, meaning a chosen fraction of all relevant documents. That sounds objective, but it hides the reason for the task. Missing one patent document may be much more costly than reading ten extra candidates. In another review setting, the cost of more screening may dominate once the likely remaining value is low. The difficulty is therefore not only estimating relevance. It is comparing two unlike things: the uncertain benefit of finding more relevant material and the concrete cost of continuing to read.
naive: A smart beginner would choose a fixed target such as stop when we think we have found 95 percent of the relevant documents. This is appealing because it turns stopping into a clean counting problem. It fails because the same percentage can mean different practical consequences in different jobs. Another beginner might stop after the search scores become low or after a long run of nonrelevant documents. That also fails because low score is not the same as low value. If the next relevant document would strongly change a patent or medical conclusion, even a small chance may justify continuing. If the payoff is modest and review time is expensive, the same chance may not. A task-blind rule cannot price these consequences.
ap: The paper's core idea is to turn stopping into a decision problem. A decision problem begins by naming the available actions, the uncertain facts, and the costs and rewards attached to outcomes. Here the action is simple: review more results or stop now. The uncertain fact is whether unseen documents still contain relevant evidence worth finding. The cost is the effort of examining additional documents. The reward, or avoided loss, is the value of finding relevant material that would otherwise be missed. The paper uses Expected Value of Perfect Information, which asks a plain question: how much would it be worth to know the hidden answer before acting? If perfect knowledge about the remaining documents would not be worth the cost of acquiring more evidence, stopping is reasonable. From this idea, the authors derive three practical stopping policies and test them on patent examining and medical systematic review tasks.
mech: The mechanism begins with a screened search result list for a professional task. Some documents have already been reviewed, so the system has evidence about how many useful documents have appeared and how the ranked list is behaving. The task also supplies a cost and payoff setting: reading another document consumes expert effort, while discovering a relevant document produces value or avoids harm. The method then considers the choice at the current point in the review. Stopping gives an immediate saving in review effort but risks leaving relevant documents unseen. Continuing buys more information, because the next reviewed documents reveal whether useful evidence remains. The Expected Value of Perfect Information step imagines the best possible version of that uncertainty: if the searcher could know the hidden relevance status of remaining material before deciding, how much better could the decision become? That value becomes a measuring stick for whether further review is worth buying. The paper derives three stopping policies from this decision-theoretic view, so the exact rule can be made practical rather than requiring impossible perfect knowledge. Each policy estimates whether the expected gain from more screening exceeds the expected cost under the current task's assumptions. The output is a recommendation to stop or continue. In experiments, those recommendations are judged not only by recall but by net utility, meaning the final balance of benefits and costs under the evaluated settings.
math: The main mathematical idea is decision theory: a way to choose among actions when each action has uncertain consequences. It does not ask only what is most likely. It asks what each possible outcome is worth or costs. In this paper, the actions are stop and continue, the uncertain state is the relevance of unseen documents, and the score is net utility, the benefit left after subtracting costs. A second idea is expected value. Expected value means averaging possible outcomes after weighting them by how likely they are. If there is a small chance of a very valuable document, that chance can still matter; if the chance is tiny and review cost is high, it may not. A third idea is the value of information. Information has value when learning it can change the action a rational searcher would take. Perfect information is an idealized upper bound: it asks what the decision would be worth if uncertainty disappeared. The paper uses that ideal to derive practical stopping policies. This math fits because screening is a sequential choice under partial sight. The central tradeoff is recall versus effort, but the paper makes that tradeoff task-specific instead of pretending one recall target has the same meaning everywhere.
dots: In the repo's broader map, this paper sits inside information retrieval and search, but it shifts attention from ranking documents to deciding when enough evidence has been gathered. It connects to ranking because the reviewed documents arrive in an order created by a search system, and errors near the top or near the stopping boundary matter more than errors buried far below. It connects to probability because the searcher must estimate what may remain unseen from partial evidence. It connects to optimization in the plain sense of choosing an action that improves a stated score: continue only when the likely value justifies the cost. It also sits near evaluation work because the abstract judges methods by net utility rather than by relevance alone. Neighboring retrieval papers ask which documents to retrieve, how to order them, or how much context to pass forward. This paper asks the next operational question: once documents are being screened by people, when should the process end?
ww: The approach should work better than a fixed recall rule because it measures the thing the user actually cares about. Recall treats every missed relevant document as the same kind of error and every extra reviewed document as outside the main target. Professional screening does not work that way. The point of reading is to support a downstream decision, and the cost of reading is paid by scarce expert labor. By putting both sides into the same decision calculation, the method can recommend longer review when the remaining possible evidence is valuable enough and earlier stopping when further evidence is unlikely to repay its cost. Expected Value of Perfect Information is useful because it gives a disciplined way to ask whether uncertainty is worth reducing. If even perfect knowledge would add little value, then spending more effort to reduce uncertainty is hard to justify. If hidden documents could change the decision enough, continued review remains worthwhile. The paper's experiments support this logic by showing higher net utility than existing stopping methods under the evaluated cost and payoff settings.
po: The payoff is a stopping decision that is tied to the professional purpose of screening. The abstract reports experiments on CLEF-IP patent data and medical systematic review datasets. Under the evaluated cost and payoff settings, the decision-theoretic policies generally produce more appropriate stopping decisions than existing methods, shown by higher net utility. The practical capability is not merely finding more relevant documents. It is knowing when extra review is no longer worth the expert effort for the task at hand. That can save time when continuing has low value and protect quality when missing documents would be costly.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The cost and payoff settings must reflect the real task; if they are wrong, the stopping rule can faithfully optimize the wrong tradeoff. The method also depends on the evidence available during screening being informative about unseen documents. If the ranking system is badly calibrated, if relevant documents are scattered unpredictably, or if the datasets differ from the deployment setting, the expected values may mislead. The abstract reports results on patent examining and systematic review datasets, but it does not prove the same behavior for every domain, every review protocol, or every way of valuing missed evidence. It also does not specify from the abstract alone how users should choose the costs and payoffs in contested real cases.
